papers.title: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners
papers.abstract: Recent work has demonstrated substantial gains on many NLP tasks and benchmarks by pre-training on a large corpus of text followed by fine-tuning on a specific task. While typically task-agnostic in architecture, this method still requires task-specific fine-tuning datasets of thousands or tens of thousands of examples. By contrast, humans can generally perform a new language task from only a few examples or from simple instructions. We show that scaling up language models greatly improves task-agnostic, few-shot performance, sometimes even reaching competitiveness with prior state-of-the-art fine-tuning approaches. Specifically, we train GPT-3, an autoregressive language model with 175 billion parameters, 10 times more than any previous non-sparse language model, and test its performance in the few-shot setting. For all tasks, GPT-3 is applied without any gradient updates or fine-tuning, with tasks and few-shot demonstrations specified purely via text interaction with the model. GPT-3 achieves strong performance on many NLP datasets, including translation, question answering, and cloze tasks, as well as several tasks that require on-the-fly reasoning or domain adaptation. At the same time, we identify some datasets where GPT-3's few-shot learning still struggles, as well as some datasets where GPT-3 faces methodological issues related to training on large web corpora.

sections.title: Introduction
paragraphs: The recent trend in natural language processing has been to pre-train a large model on a broad corpus and then fine-tune it on a downstream task. This recipe has produced large gains on benchmarks such as SuperGLUE, but it requires a labeled dataset for every task and a separate model for every task. In this paper we study a different setting: a single model is given only a natural language description of the task and a small number of demonstrations, and it must perform the task without any parameter updates. We call this in-context learning.

We train GPT-3, a 175 billion parameter autoregressive language model, and evaluate it on more than 40 benchmarks in this few-shot setting. The model has 96 layers, a hidden size of 12288, 96 attention heads, and a context window of 2048 tokens. Training used 10000 NVIDIA V100 GPUs and roughly 300 billion tokens drawn from a mixture of Common Crawl, WebText2, Books1, Books2, and Wikipedia. To our knowledge this is the largest dense language model trained to date.

sections.title: Approach
paragraphs: Our approach combines a scaled-up Transformer language model with a evaluation protocol that requires no fine-tuning. We describe the few-shot setting, the model architecture, and the training data in the following subsections.

sections.title: Few-Shot Setting
paragraphs: We evaluate the model in three settings. In zero-shot learning the model is given only a task description and no examples. In one-shot learning it is given one demonstration, and in few-shot learning it is given a small number of demonstrations, typically between 10 and 100. In all cases the demonstrations are concatenated into the prompt, and the model generates the answer autoregressively. No gradient updates are performed, and the same model is used for every task.

This protocol has the advantage that it measures the ability of a single model to adapt to new tasks at inference time, which is much closer to how humans use language. It also removes the need for task-specific architectures and large labeled datasets. The protocol has the disadvantage that the choice of prompt and demonstrations can strongly affect performance, and we therefore report results for several prompt formats where possible.

sections.title: Model and Architecture
paragraphs: GPT-3 is an autoregressive Transformer language model with 175 billion parameters, 96 layers, a hidden size of 12288, and 96 attention heads. It uses alternating dense and locally banded sparse attention layers, and the context window is 2048 tokens. The model is trained with the same objective as GPT-2, namely predicting the next token, and no task-specific heads are added. Table 1 compares the eight model sizes that we train, from 125 million to 175 billion parameters.

We use a byte-level byte pair encoding vocabulary of 50257 tokens. The model is trained with a batch size of 3.2 million tokens, a learning rate that is warmed up over the first 1 percent of training and then decayed, and mixed precision. Training the largest model required 10000 NVIDIA V100 GPUs and roughly 300 billion tokens; the total compute is about 3.14e23 FLOPs. We do not fine-tune the model on any downstream task.

sections.title: Training Data
paragraphs: The training data is a mixture of five corpora: Common Crawl, which is filtered and deduplicated; WebText2, the extended version of the WebText corpus used to train GPT-2; Books1 and Books2, two book corpora; and Wikipedia. The mixture is sampled with weights that favor higher-quality sources, and the total amount of training data is roughly 300 billion tokens. We remove benchmark test sets from the training data to avoid contamination, and we report the results of a contamination analysis in the appendix.

sections.title: Results
paragraphs: We evaluate GPT-3 on language modeling, question answering, reading comprehension, translation, commonsense reasoning, and arithmetic. In this section we highlight a few representative results; the full set of results is reported in the appendix. Across tasks, performance improves smoothly with model size, and the largest model is often competitive with fine-tuned systems.

sections.title: Language Modeling and Cloze Tasks
paragraphs: On LAMBADA, GPT-3 achieves 86.4 percent accuracy in the few-shot setting, compared with 63.24 percent for GPT-2. On the Children's Book Test the model achieves 90.1 percent accuracy, and on HellaSwag it achieves 78.9 percent. These results show that the ability to use long-range context continues to improve with scale, and that in-context learning is particularly effective for cloze-style tasks.

sections.title: Question Answering
paragraphs: On TriviaQA, GPT-3 achieves 71.2 percent accuracy in the few-shot setting, which is comparable to the performance of fine-tuned models that use retrieval. On the OpenBookQA and ARC datasets the model also performs well, although it struggles on questions that require multi-step reasoning. Table 2 summarizes the results on these benchmarks.

sections.title: SuperGLUE and Natural Language Inference
paragraphs: On SuperGLUE, GPT-3 achieves an average score of 87.8 in the few-shot setting, which is close to the performance of fine-tuned models and well above the previous zero-shot state of the art. The largest gains come from tasks that can be formatted as cloze questions, such as BoolQ and MultiRC, while tasks that require careful handling of entailment labels remain difficult.

sections.title: Arithmetic and Symbolic Reasoning
paragraphs: GPT-3 can perform two-digit addition and subtraction with high accuracy when given a few worked examples, but its accuracy drops sharply for three-digit arithmetic and for problems that require carrying. On the MATH dataset the model performs poorly, which suggests that in-context learning does not by itself provide the systematicity needed for multi-step mathematics.

sections.title: Translation
paragraphs: On WMT-14 English-to-French translation, GPT-3 achieves 32.6 BLEU in the few-shot setting, compared with 11.5 BLEU for GPT-2. On English-to-German the model achieves 24.0 BLEU. These results are below the best supervised systems, but they show that a language model trained mostly on English can translate with only a handful of demonstrations.

sections.title: Limitations
paragraphs: GPT-3 has several important limitations. First, despite its strong performance on many benchmarks, it still struggles on tasks that require multi-step reasoning, such as arithmetic with large numbers and commonsense reasoning about physical situations. Second, its performance is sensitive to the prompt format, and small changes in wording can produce large changes in accuracy.

Third, the model was trained on a large web corpus, which introduces the risk of memorizing benchmark data and of reproducing biases present in the training text. Fourth, the model is expensive to train and to serve, and its energy consumption is substantial. Finally, like other autoregressive models, GPT-3 can generate fluent but false statements, and it provides no calibrated confidence estimates.

sections.title: Broader Impact
paragraphs: Large language models have the potential to be used for beneficial applications such as writing assistance, translation, and accessibility. They also have the potential to be misused for spam generation, disinformation, and impersonation. Because the model can generate text that is indistinguishable from human writing, it may become difficult to attribute content to its author. We believe that the release of large models should be accompanied by careful analysis of these risks and by mitigations such as output filtering and watermarking.

sections.title: Conclusion
paragraphs: We have shown that a single 175 billion parameter language model can perform a wide range of tasks in the few-shot setting, without any fine-tuning or task-specific architecture. Performance improves smoothly with scale, and on some benchmarks GPT-3 is competitive with fine-tuned systems. At the same time, the model has clear limitations in reasoning, robustness, and efficiency. We believe that scaling up language models is a promising direction, but that it must be combined with better training objectives, retrieval, and evaluation methods to produce systems that are reliable and useful.

papers.title: Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition
papers.short_title: Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition
papers.abstract: Deeper neural networks are more difficult to train. We present a residual learning framework to ease the training of networks that are substantially deeper than those used previously. We explicitly reformulate the layers as learning residual functions with reference to the layer inputs, instead of learning unreferenced functions. We provide comprehensive empirical evidence showing that these residual networks are easier to optimize, and can gain accuracy from considerably increased depth. On the ImageNet dataset we evaluate residual nets with a depth of up to 152 layers, 8 times deeper than VGG nets but still having lower complexity. An ensemble of these residual nets achieves 3.57 percent top-5 error on the ImageNet test set. This result won the 1st place on the ILSVRC 2015 classification task. We also present analysis on CIFAR-10 with 100 and 1000 layers. The depth of representations is of central importance for many visual recognition tasks, and our residual nets are easy to optimize even at 152 layers.

sections.title: Introduction
paragraphs: Deep convolutional neural networks have led to a series of breakthroughs in image classification. The depth of the network is of crucial importance for many visual recognition tasks, and the empirical evidence from AlexNet, VGG, and GoogLeNet shows that deeper networks achieve better accuracy. However, simply stacking more layers does not always improve performance: very deep plain networks suffer from the degradation problem, in which accuracy saturates and then degrades as depth increases.

In this paper we address the degradation problem with a residual learning framework. Instead of hoping that a stack of layers directly fits a desired underlying mapping, we explicitly let these layers fit a residual mapping. We show that it is easier to optimize the residual mapping than to optimize the original unreferenced mapping, and that extremely deep residual networks can be trained efficiently. On ImageNet we train a 152-layer residual network and obtain 3.57 percent top-5 error with an ensemble, winning the ILSVRC 2015 classification task.

sections.title: Related Work
paragraphs: Our work is related to the classical VGG and GoogLeNet architectures, which showed that depth and careful design are critical for recognition accuracy. VGG nets use 16 to 19 layers and a very uniform architecture, while GoogLeNet uses 22 layers and an inception module. Both are much deeper than AlexNet, which has 8 layers, and both improve accuracy substantially. Our residual networks can be seen as a generalization of these architectures in which shortcut connections are added to every few stacked layers.

Shortcut connections have been studied in the context of highway networks, which use gated shortcuts, and in the context of multi-layer perceptrons with auxiliary classifiers. Our formulation differs in that the shortcut connections are identity mappings with no parameters, which keeps the model simple and makes it possible to train networks with more than 100 layers. The degradation problem has also been observed in the context of recurrent networks, where gated architectures such as LSTM are used to ease optimization.

sections.title: Deep Residual Learning
paragraphs: We formulate residual learning as follows. Let H(x) denote the desired underlying mapping to be fit by a few stacked layers, with x denoting the inputs to the first of these layers. We let the stacked layers fit a residual mapping F(x) = H(x) - x, so that the original mapping becomes F(x) + x. The hypothesis is that it is easier to optimize the residual mapping than the original mapping, and in the extreme case where an identity mapping is optimal, it is easier to push the residual to zero than to fit an identity mapping by a stack of nonlinear layers.

sections.title: Residual Learning
paragraphs: The degradation problem suggests that solvers might have difficulties in approximating identity mappings by multiple nonlinear layers. With the residual learning reformulation, if the identity mapping is optimal, the solvers may simply drive the weights of the nonlinear layers toward zero to approximate the identity mapping. In real cases, it is unlikely that the identity mappings are optimal, but the reformulation may help precondition the problem and ease optimization.

We test this hypothesis on ImageNet with plain networks of 18 and 34 layers. The 34-layer plain network has higher training error than the 18-layer plain network, which confirms that the degradation is not caused by overfitting. When we add shortcut connections, the 34-layer residual network achieves lower training error and better accuracy than the 18-layer network, which demonstrates that residual learning eases optimization at increased depth.

sections.title: Identity Mapping by Shortcuts
paragraphs: We adopt residual learning to every few stacked layers. A building block is defined as y = F(x, W_i) + x, where x and y are the input and output vectors of the layers considered, and F is the residual function to be learned. The function F + x is realized by a shortcut connection that performs element-wise addition, and the shortcut introduces neither extra parameters nor extra computation. When the dimensions of x and F change, we perform a linear projection W_s x on the shortcut to match dimensions, as in Equation (2).

The form of the residual function F is flexible. In this paper we use a stack of two or three layers, and more layers are possible. If F has only a single layer, the block resembles a linear projection and the shortcut is not very useful, so we use at least two layers. The identity shortcut is sufficient to address the degradation problem, and it is computationally cheap, so we prefer it whenever the dimensions match.

sections.title: Network Architectures
paragraphs: We compare plain networks and residual networks on ImageNet. The plain network is inspired by VGG and consists of 3x3 convolutions with a fixed number of filters per feature map size, downsampling by stride 2, and a global average pooling layer followed by a fully connected layer with softmax. The residual network adds shortcut connections to every pair of 3x3 convolutions. Table 1 summarizes the architectures of the 34-layer and 152-layer residual networks.

The 34-layer residual network has 3.6 billion FLOPs, which is only 18 percent of the 19-layer VGG network, and the 152-layer network has 11.3 billion FLOPs, still lower than VGG-19. We use batch normalization after every convolution and before the activation, and we initialize the weights as in He et al. (2015). The networks are trained with stochastic gradient descent, a batch size of 256, and a weight decay of 0.0001.

sections.title: Implementation
paragraphs: We train the networks on the ImageNet 2012 classification dataset, which contains 1.28 million training images and 50,000 validation images in 1000 classes. We follow the data augmentation of AlexNet: a 224x224 crop is randomly sampled from an image or its horizontal flip, and the per-pixel mean is subtracted. We use stochastic gradient descent with momentum 0.9, a batch size of 256, and an initial learning rate of 0.1 that is divided by 10 when the validation error plateaus. The models are trained for up to 60 epochs on 8 GPUs, and training a 152-layer network takes approximately 3.5 days on this hardware.

At test time we adopt the standard 10-crop testing and average the softmax scores over the crops. For the best results we also average the predictions of multiple scales. We do not use any additional training data, and all results are reported on the ImageNet validation set unless stated otherwise.

sections.title: Experiments
paragraphs: We conduct experiments on ImageNet, CIFAR-10, and the COCO object detection benchmark. On ImageNet the residual networks outperform both plain networks and the previous best architectures, and the 152-layer model achieves 3.57 percent top-5 error when used in an ensemble. On CIFAR-10 we train networks with 100 and 1000 layers and show that residual learning remains effective at extreme depth. On COCO the residual networks improve object detection over the VGG-based baseline.

sections.title: ImageNet Classification
paragraphs: Table 2 reports the ImageNet classification results. The plain 34-layer network has higher validation error than the plain 18-layer network, which confirms the degradation problem. The 34-layer residual network, which is the baseline for our deeper models, achieves 3.57 percent top-5 error in the single-model setting, and the 152-layer residual network achieves 3.57 percent top-5 error when combined into an ensemble. The 152-layer single model achieves 4.49 percent top-5 error, which is already better than the previous best single-model result.

The improvement over VGG and GoogLeNet is consistent across top-1 and top-5 error, and it comes without an increase in computational cost: the 152-layer network has fewer FLOPs than VGG-19. These results show that residual learning makes it possible to benefit from depth without suffering from the degradation problem.

sections.title: CIFAR-10 and Analysis
paragraphs: On CIFAR-10 we train residual networks with 20, 32, 44, 56, 110, and 1202 layers. The 110-layer network achieves 6.43 percent error, which is comparable to the best reported results at the time, and the 1202-layer network achieves 7.93 percent error, showing that residual learning remains trainable at extreme depth. The training error of the 1202-layer network is lower than that of the 110-layer network, which indicates that the deeper model is not underfitting.

sections.title: Object Detection on COCO
paragraphs: We apply the residual networks as the backbone of Faster R-CNN on the COCO dataset. Replacing the VGG-16 backbone with ResNet-101 improves the COCO mAP by 3.1 points, and the improvement is consistent across object sizes. This result suggests that the gains from residual learning transfer beyond image classification to dense prediction tasks.

sections.title: Conclusion
paragraphs: We have presented a residual learning framework that eases the training of extremely deep networks. Our residual networks are easy to optimize and gain accuracy from increased depth, and they achieve state-of-the-art results on ImageNet, CIFAR-10, and COCO. We believe that residual learning is a general technique that can be applied to other network architectures and other recognition tasks.

appendix.title: Appendix: Architectures for CIFAR-10
paragraphs: The CIFAR-10 networks use a 3x3 convolution with 16 filters followed by three stages of 2n blocks with 16, 32, and 64 filters, where n is the number of blocks per stage. Each block consists of two 3x3 convolutions with batch normalization and ReLU, plus an identity shortcut. Downsampling is performed by the first block of stages 2 and 3 with stride 2. The networks are trained for 200 epochs with a batch size of 128 and a learning rate of 0.1 that is divided by 10 at epochs 100 and 150.

For the 1202-layer network we use the same architecture with n = 200 blocks in the first stage. The network is trained with the same hyperparameters as the smaller models, and it converges without difficulty. The training error of the 1202-layer network is 0.1 percent, which is lower than that of the 110-layer network, confirming that residual learning addresses the degradation problem even at extreme depth.

papers.title: ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks
papers.abstract: We trained a large, deep convolutional neural network to classify the 1.2 million high-resolution images in the ImageNet LSVRC-2010 contest into the 1000 different classes. On the test data, we achieved top-1 and top-5 error rates of 37.5 percent and 15.3 percent, which is considerably better than the previous state-of-the-art. The neural network, which has 60 million parameters and 650,000 neurons, consists of five convolutional layers, some of which are followed by max-pooling layers, and three fully-connected layers with a final 1000-way softmax. To make training faster, we used non-saturating neurons and a very efficient GPU implementation of the convolution operation. To reduce overfitting in the fully-connected layers we employed a recently developed regularization method called dropout, with a rate of 0.5. We also used data augmentation and local response normalization. The network was trained on two GTX 580 3GB GPUs for five to six days.

sections.title: Introduction
paragraphs: Current approaches to object recognition make essential use of machine learning methods. To improve their performance, we can collect larger datasets, learn more powerful models, and use better techniques for preventing overfitting. Until recently, labeled image datasets were relatively small, on the order of tens of thousands of images, so recognition systems relied heavily on hand-engineered features. The ImageNet dataset, with more than 15 million labeled high-resolution images in over 22,000 categories, changed this picture.

In this paper we train a deep convolutional neural network on the ImageNet LSVRC-2010 dataset and show that a large, purely supervised model can substantially outperform hand-engineered feature pipelines. Our network has 60 million parameters and 650,000 neurons, and it is trained on two GTX 580 3GB GPUs for five to six days. We use ReLU nonlinearities, dropout with rate 0.5, data augmentation, and local response normalization, and we achieve 15.3 percent top-5 error on the test set.

sections.title: The Dataset
paragraphs: ImageNet is a dataset of over 15 million labeled high-resolution images belonging to roughly 22,000 categories. The images were collected from the web and labeled by human labelers using Amazon's Mechanical Turk. The ILSVRC-2010 subset contains 1.2 million training images, 50,000 validation images, and 150,000 test images in 1000 classes. Because the test set labels are not publicly available, we report results on the validation set for most experiments, and we use the test set only for the final ILSVRC submission.

The images vary substantially in resolution, and we therefore down-sample the images to a fixed resolution of 256x256. For training we randomly crop 224x224 patches from the images and their horizontal reflections, and at test time we extract five 224x224 patches plus their reflections and average the predictions. This preprocessing is the only domain-specific engineering in our system.

sections.title: The Architecture
paragraphs: The network contains eight learned layers: five convolutional layers and three fully-connected layers. The convolutional layers use filters of size 11x11, 5x5, and 3x3, and the fully-connected layers have 4096, 4096, and 1000 units respectively. The last layer is a softmax over the 1000 classes, and the objective is the multinomial logistic regression loss, as in Equation (1). We describe the non-standard choices below.

sections.title: ReLU Nonlinearity
paragraphs: The standard way to model a neuron's output f as a function of its input x is with f(x) = tanh(x) or f(x) = (1 + e^-x)^-1. In terms of training time with gradient descent, these saturating nonlinearities are much slower than the non-saturating nonlinearity f(x) = max(0, x), which we call a rectified linear unit (ReLU). We use ReLUs throughout the network, and we find that deep convolutional networks train several times faster with ReLUs than with tanh units.

This speedup is important because it allows us to train a much larger network on the same hardware. We do not use any unsupervised pre-training, and the network is trained end-to-end with backpropagation.

sections.title: Training on Multiple GPUs
paragraphs: A single GTX 580 has only 3GB of memory, which is too small to train the full network. We therefore spread the network across two GPUs, placing half of the neurons in each GPU and communicating between them only at certain layers. This scheme allows us to train a network that would not fit on a single GPU, and it slightly reduces the training time because the GPUs can work in parallel. We use two GTX 580 3GB GPUs, and training the network takes five to six days.

sections.title: Local Response Normalization
paragraphs: ReLUs have the desirable property that they do not require input normalization to prevent them from saturating. However, we still find that local response normalization helps generalization. The normalization is applied across neighboring feature maps at the same spatial position, and it implements a form of lateral inhibition. We use the normalization after the first and second convolutional layers, and it reduces the top-1 error by roughly 1.4 percentage points.

sections.title: Overlapping Pooling
paragraphs: The pooling layers in our network overlap: the pooling window is 3x3 and the stride is 2, whereas the traditional non-overlapping pooling uses a window and stride of 2. Overlapping pooling slightly reduces the top-1 and top-5 error, and it also reduces the number of parameters in the network. We use overlapping pooling in all of the pooling layers.

sections.title: Overall Architecture
paragraphs: The network is composed of five convolutional layers followed by three fully-connected layers. The first convolutional layer filters the 224x224x3 input image with 96 kernels of size 11x11x3 with a stride of 4 pixels, and the second layer takes the output of the first as input and filters it with 256 kernels of size 5x5x48. The third, fourth, and fifth layers are connected without any intervening pooling or normalization layers. Table 1 summarizes the sizes and shapes of each layer, and Figure 1 shows the overall architecture.

The output of the fifth convolutional layer is flattened and passed to a fully-connected layer with 4096 units, then to another fully-connected layer with 4096 units, and finally to a 1000-way softmax. The total number of parameters is 60 million, of which roughly 58 million are in the fully-connected layers. The network is trained with stochastic gradient descent with a batch size of 128, momentum 0.9, and weight decay 0.0005, and the learning rate is initialized to 0.01 and reduced by a factor of 10 when the validation error stops improving.

sections.title: Reducing Overfitting
paragraphs: The network has 60 million parameters, which is far more than the number of training images, so overfitting is a serious concern. We use two main techniques to reduce overfitting: data augmentation and dropout. Together they roughly double the effective size of the training set and substantially improve generalization.

sections.title: Data Augmentation
paragraphs: The easiest and most common method to reduce overfitting is to artificially enlarge the dataset using label-preserving transformations. We use two forms of data augmentation: random crops and horizontal reflections, and altering the intensities of the RGB channels. At test time we average the predictions over ten patches, and this averaging reduces the top-1 error by about 0.5 percent.

The second form of data augmentation consists of changing the intensities of the RGB channels in training images. We perform PCA on the set of RGB pixel values across the ImageNet training set, and we add multiples of the principal components to each training image. This scheme approximates the important property of natural images, namely that object identity is invariant to changes in the intensity and color of the illumination.

sections.title: Dropout
paragraphs: Combining the predictions of many different models is a very successful way to reduce test errors, but it is expensive to train many models. Dropout is a much cheaper method: it randomly sets the output of each hidden neuron to zero with probability 0.5, so that the network samples a different architecture at each training step. At test time we use all of the neurons but multiply their outputs by 0.5, which approximates the geometric mean of the predictions of the exponentially many thinned networks.

We use dropout with rate 0.5 in the first two fully-connected layers. Without dropout, the network overfits badly and the validation error is several percentage points higher. Dropout roughly doubles the number of iterations required to converge, but it substantially improves test accuracy.

sections.title: Results
paragraphs: On the ILSVRC-2010 test set, our network achieves top-1 and top-5 error rates of 37.5 percent and 15.3 percent, which is substantially better than the previous best result of 45.7 percent and 25.7 percent. On the ILSVRC-2012 validation set the network achieves 15.3 percent top-5 error, and on the test set it achieves 15.3 percent top-5 error as part of the winning team entry.

sections.title: Qualitative Results
paragraphs: Figure 2 shows the learned convolutional filters. The filters learned by the first layer are oriented edges and color blobs, similar to the filters learned by sparse coding and Gabor filters. The filters in the higher layers are more complex and respond to textures and object parts. The network's predictions are often semantically reasonable even when they are wrong, which suggests that it has learned a rich representation of the visual world.

sections.title: Comparison with Prior Work
paragraphs: Table 2 compares our results with the best entries from ILSVRC-2010 and ILSVRC-2012. Our network improves the top-5 error by more than 10 percentage points over the previous best method, and it does so with a single model rather than an ensemble. The result demonstrated that deep convolutional networks trained on GPUs could outperform feature-engineering pipelines on large-scale recognition.

sections.title: Discussion
paragraphs: Our results show that a large deep convolutional neural network is capable of achieving record-breaking performance on a challenging object recognition task. The key ingredients are a large labeled dataset, a deep architecture with ReLU nonlinearities, efficient GPU implementations of convolution, and regularization by dropout and data augmentation. We did not use any unsupervised pre-training, and the network was trained end-to-end.

One limitation of our approach is that the network is expensive to train and requires a large amount of memory, which is why we split it across two GPUs. Another limitation is that the architecture was designed by hand and required many experiments to tune. In future work it would be interesting to explore deeper networks, better initialization, and automatically searched architectures.

paragraphs: The network was trained with stochastic gradient descent with a batch size of 128, momentum 0.9, and weight decay 0.0005. papers.title: An Image is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale
papers.abstract: While the Transformer architecture has become the de-facto standard for natural language processing tasks, its applications to computer vision remain limited. In vision, attention is either applied in conjunction with convolutional networks, or used to replace certain components of convolutional networks while keeping their overall structure in place. We show that this reliance on CNNs is not necessary and a pure transformer applied directly to sequences of image patches can perform very well on image classification tasks. When pre-trained on large amounts of data and transferred to multiple mid-sized or small image recognition benchmarks, Vision Transformer (ViT) attains excellent results compared to state-of-the-art convolutional networks while requiring substantially fewer computational resources to train. Our largest model, ViT-H/14, has 632 million parameters, uses 16x16 patches, and was pre-trained on 32 TPUv3 cores; it reaches 88.55 percent top-1 accuracy on ImageNet when fine-tuned.

sections.title: Introduction
paragraphs: Self-attention-based architectures, in particular Transformers, have become the model of choice in natural language processing. The dominant approach is to pre-train on a large text corpus and then fine-tune on a smaller task-specific dataset. In computer vision, however, convolutional architectures remain dominant. Attention mechanisms have been added to convolutional networks, or used to replace some components, but the overall structure of the convolutional network has been kept.

In this paper we show that a pure Transformer applied directly to sequences of image patches can perform very well on image classification. We split an image into fixed-size patches, linearly embed each patch, add position embeddings, and feed the resulting sequence to a standard Transformer encoder. We call this model the Vision Transformer, or ViT. When pre-trained on large datasets and transferred to smaller benchmarks, ViT matches or outperforms state-of-the-art convolutional networks while requiring substantially fewer computational resources to train.

sections.title: Related Work
paragraphs: Transformers were introduced for machine translation and have since become the standard architecture for language understanding. The key ingredient is self-attention, which allows each position to attend to all other positions in a sequence. Scaling Transformers to images requires a way to convert the two-dimensional image into a one-dimensional sequence, and the most natural choice is to split the image into patches.

Prior work has applied attention to images in several ways. Some models combine convolutional feature maps with attention, while others use attention to replace pooling or to model long-range dependencies. Our model differs in that it uses no convolutions at all: the patch embeddings are linear projections, and all spatial reasoning is performed by the Transformer. This makes the architecture simple and allows it to be trained with the same recipe as a language model.

sections.title: Method
paragraphs: We follow the standard Transformer encoder as closely as possible. The model receives a sequence of patch embeddings, processes it with alternating multi-head self-attention and MLP blocks, and produces a classification prediction from a special token. The only image-specific components are the patch extraction and the position embeddings.

sections.title: Vision Transformer
paragraphs: An image is split into a grid of non-overlapping patches. For a 224x224 image and 16x16 patches, this produces 196 patches. Each patch is flattened and linearly projected to a vector of dimension d_model, and the resulting sequence is prepended with a learnable classification token. Position embeddings are added to the patch embeddings to retain spatial information, and the sequence is passed through a standard Transformer encoder with alternating multi-head attention and MLP blocks. Equation (1) shows the attention operation, and Equation (2) shows the patch embedding.

The Transformer encoder consists of L layers, each with multi-head self-attention and a position-wise MLP. Layer normalization is applied before each block, and residual connections are used around each block. The classification token output is passed through a linear layer to produce the class logits. Table 1 summarizes the three model variants, ViT-Base, ViT-Large, and ViT-Huge.

sections.title: Fine-tuning and Few-shot Learning
paragraphs: We pre-train the model on a large dataset and then fine-tune it on the target dataset. For fine-tuning we replace the classification head with a new linear layer and train all parameters for a small number of epochs. We also evaluate the model in a few-shot setting, in which only a few training examples per class are available, and in a linear probe setting, in which the encoder is frozen and only a linear classifier is trained.

When the target dataset is much smaller than the pre-training dataset, fine-tuning the whole model can overfit. In that case we found it better to use a higher learning rate for the newly initialized head and a smaller learning rate for the pre-trained encoder. We also use RandAugment and mixup during fine-tuning, and we remove them when the target dataset is very small.

sections.title: Experiments
paragraphs: We evaluate ViT on ImageNet, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Oxford Flowers-102, and the VTAB suite. We first compare the model to state-of-the-art convolutional networks when pre-trained on large datasets, and then study the effect of pre-training data size, model scale, and patch size.

sections.title: Setup
paragraphs: We pre-train on ImageNet-21k, which contains 14 million images in 21,843 classes, and on JFT-300M, which contains 303 million images in 18,000 classes. We use Adam with beta_1 = 0.9 and beta_2 = 0.999, a batch size of 4096, and a weight decay of 0.1, and we train for 300,000 steps with a cosine learning rate schedule. The largest model, ViT-H/14, has 632 million parameters and was trained on 32 TPUv3 cores. For fine-tuning we use SGD with momentum 0.9, a batch size of 512, and 10 epochs.

sections.title: Comparison with State of the Art
paragraphs: When pre-trained on JFT-300M, ViT-H/14 achieves 88.55 percent top-1 accuracy on ImageNet when fine-tuned, which is comparable to the best convolutional networks while requiring substantially less pre-training compute. On CIFAR-100 it achieves 93.2 percent, on Oxford Flowers-102 it achieves 99.4 percent, and on the VTAB suite it achieves 77.9 percent. Table 2 summarizes the ImageNet results for the three ViT variants.

The results are particularly strong when the pre-training dataset is large. With ImageNet-21k pre-training, ViT-L/16 achieves 85.3 percent top-1 accuracy, which is slightly below the best convolutional networks, but with JFT-300M pre-training the same model reaches 87.8 percent. This suggests that the inductive bias of convolutions is useful when data is limited, but that Transformers can learn appropriate inductive biases from sufficiently large datasets.

sections.title: Pre-training Data
paragraphs: We study how the pre-training dataset size affects performance. ViT-L/16 pre-trained on ImageNet-21k performs worse than the same model pre-trained on JFT-300M, and the gap is larger for smaller datasets. On the smaller datasets, the model benefits from stronger regularization and from a larger patch size, which reduces the sequence length and the number of parameters.

sections.title: Scaling Study
paragraphs: We train models of different sizes and patch sizes on JFT-300M and measure their transfer performance. Performance improves with model size and with smaller patch size, but the computational cost grows quickly. The 16x16 patch size gives the best trade-off between accuracy and compute for the model sizes we consider, and the 32x32 patch size is cheaper but less accurate.

sections.title: Inspecting Vision Transformer
paragraphs: We visualize the learned position embeddings and the attention maps. The position embeddings learn to represent the two-dimensional structure of the image, and the attention maps show that the model attends to semantically relevant regions. In the lower layers, attention often attends to nearby patches, while in the higher layers it attends to objects and their parts, which is consistent with the behavior of convolutional networks.

sections.title: Conclusion
paragraphs: We have shown that a pure Transformer can be applied directly to images and can match or outperform state-of-the-art convolutional networks on image classification when pre-trained on large datasets. The Vision Transformer is simple and scalable, and it opens the door to using the same architecture for vision and language. Future work should study self-supervised pre-training, video, and detection, where the benefits of large-scale pre-training may be even greater.

papers.title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models
papers.short_title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models
papers.abstract: An important paradigm of natural language processing consists of large-scale pre-training on general domain data followed by adaptation to particular tasks or domains. As we pre-train larger models, full fine-tuning, which retrains all model parameters, becomes less feasible. Using GPT-3 175B as an example, deploying independent instances of fine-tuned models, each with 175B parameters, is prohibitively expensive. We propose Low-Rank Adaptation, or LoRA, which freezes the pre-trained model weights and injects trainable rank decomposition matrices into each layer of the Transformer architecture, greatly reducing the number of trainable parameters for downstream tasks. Compared to fine-tuning GPT-3 175B with Adam, LoRA reduces the number of trainable parameters by 10,000 times and the GPU memory requirement by 3 times. LoRA performs on par with or better than fine-tuning in model quality on RoBERTa, DeBERTa, GPT-2, and GPT-3, despite having fewer trainable parameters, a higher training throughput, and no additional inference latency. On GPT-3 175B, LoRA with rank r = 8 and alpha = 16 requires only 4.7 million trainable parameters.

sections.title: Introduction
paragraphs: Large pre-trained language models have become the foundation of modern natural language processing. The standard adaptation recipe is to fine-tune all parameters on a downstream dataset, which produces strong results but requires storing a full copy of the model for every task. As models grow to hundreds of billions of parameters, this approach becomes impractical: a single fine-tuned copy of GPT-3 175B is 700GB in fp16, and serving many such copies requires a proportional amount of accelerator memory.

We propose Low-Rank Adaptation, or LoRA, which freezes the pre-trained weights and learns a low-rank update for each weight matrix. The number of trainable parameters is reduced by up to 10,000 times, and the GPU memory requirement is reduced by 3 times, while model quality is preserved. Because the learned update can be merged into the original weights at inference time, LoRA introduces no additional inference latency. On GPT-3 175B, LoRA with rank r = 8 and alpha = 16 trains only 4.7 million parameters.

sections.title: Problem Statement
paragraphs: Given a pre-trained model with weights W_0, full fine-tuning learns a new weight matrix W = W_0 + Delta W for each task, where Delta W has the same dimensions as W_0. The number of trainable parameters is therefore equal to the number of parameters in the model, which is prohibitive for large models. Adapter-based methods add small trainable modules, but they introduce additional layers and therefore additional inference latency.

We hypothesize that the update to the weights during adaptation has a low intrinsic rank. If this hypothesis holds, then Delta W can be represented as the product of two much smaller matrices, and only those matrices need to be trained. This reduces the number of trainable parameters by orders of magnitude while keeping the expressivity of the full model.

sections.title: Method
paragraphs: LoRA represents the weight update as a low-rank decomposition. For a pre-trained weight matrix W_0 in R^(d x k), we learn a update Delta W = B A, where B is in R^(d x r) and A is in R^(r x k), and the rank r is much smaller than d and k. During training W_0 is frozen and only A and B receive gradient updates. The forward pass becomes h = W_0 x + Delta W x = W_0 x + B A x, as in Equation (1).

sections.title: Low-Rank Update
paragraphs: We initialize A with a random Gaussian distribution and B with zeros, so that Delta W = B A is zero at the beginning of training and the model starts from the pre-trained behavior. We scale Delta W by alpha / r, where alpha is a constant, as in Equation (2). This scaling makes it possible to change r without retuning the learning rate, and it keeps the magnitude of the update roughly constant across ranks.

The rank r is the only hyperparameter that controls the capacity of the update. In our experiments r = 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16 all perform well, and r = 8 is a good default. The choice of which weight matrices to adapt matters more than the rank: adapting both W_q and W_v gives the best results, while adapting only one of them or adapting the feed-forward layers gives smaller gains.

sections.title: Applying LoRA to Transformers
paragraphs: In the Transformer architecture there are four weight matrices in the self-attention module, W_q, W_k, W_v, and W_o, and two in the MLP module. We treat the attention weight matrices as a single matrix of size d_model x d_model and adapt it with LoRA. We keep the MLP modules frozen in most experiments, and we find that adapting W_q and W_v is sufficient to obtain most of the gains.

Because W_0 is frozen, the gradients with respect to A and B are computed from the same activations as in full fine-tuning, and the memory required for optimizer states is proportional to the number of trainable parameters rather than to the size of the model. This is the main source of the 3 times memory reduction that we observe on GPT-3 175B.

sections.title: Practical Benefits
paragraphs: LoRA has several practical benefits. First, the pre-trained weights can be shared across tasks, and only the small LoRA matrices need to be stored, which reduces storage by orders of magnitude. Second, the learned update can be merged into W_0 at inference time, so there is no additional latency. Third, training is faster because the optimizer only updates a small number of parameters. Finally, LoRA is compatible with other parameter-efficient methods such as prefix tuning.

sections.title: Experiments
paragraphs: We evaluate LoRA on GPT-3 175B, RoBERTa, DeBERTa, and GPT-2. We compare against full fine-tuning, adapter-based methods, and prefix tuning. Across benchmarks, LoRA matches or exceeds the quality of full fine-tuning while training far fewer parameters.

sections.title: Baselines
paragraphs: We compare LoRA with full fine-tuning, with adapter layers inserted after the attention and MLP modules, and with prefix tuning, which prepends trainable vectors to the keys and values. All methods are trained with the same data and evaluated on the same benchmarks. For GPT-3 175B we use 8 NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs and a batch size of 128.

sections.title: GPT-3 175B Results
paragraphs: On GPT-3 175B, LoRA with r = 8 and alpha = 16 trains 4.7 million parameters, compared with 175 billion for full fine-tuning, and reduces GPU memory by 3 times. On the WikiSQL and SAMSum benchmarks, LoRA matches or slightly exceeds the quality of full fine-tuning. Table 1 reports the number of trainable parameters and the memory usage for each method.

The results show that the low-rank hypothesis holds at the scale of GPT-3. Increasing the rank beyond 8 does not improve quality on these tasks, which suggests that the intrinsic dimension of the adaptation is small. LoRA also trains faster than full fine-tuning because the backward pass does not need to compute gradients for the frozen weights.

sections.title: GLUE Benchmark
paragraphs: On the GLUE benchmark with RoBERTa-large, LoRA achieves an average score of 91.6, compared with 91.4 for full fine-tuning, while training only 0.8 million parameters. On DeBERTa-XXL, LoRA achieves 90.8 with 0.3 million trainable parameters. These results confirm that LoRA is effective for encoder models as well as for autoregressive models.

sections.title: E2E NLG and WikiSQL
paragraphs: On the E2E NLG challenge, LoRA achieves a BLEU score of 70.4 with 0.8 million trainable parameters, compared with 70.4 for full fine-tuning. On WikiSQL, LoRA achieves 73.7 percent execution accuracy, compared with 73.2 for full fine-tuning. In both cases the gap between LoRA and full fine-tuning is within noise, even though LoRA trains less than 1 percent of the parameters.

sections.title: Related Work
paragraphs: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning has received considerable attention. Adapter methods insert small trainable modules between the layers of a pre-trained model, and prefix tuning prepends trainable vectors to the keys and values. Both approaches reduce the number of trainable parameters, but adapters add inference latency and prefix tuning reduces the effective context length. LoRA avoids both problems because the update can be merged into the original weights.

Low-rank approximations have also been used for model compression. Our work differs in that the low-rank update is learned during adaptation and is not intended to approximate the full model; instead, it captures the task-specific change in the weights. This connection suggests that the intrinsic dimensionality of adaptation is much smaller than the dimensionality of the model.

sections.title: Conclusion
paragraphs: We have presented LoRA, a simple and effective method for adapting large language models. LoRA freezes the pre-trained weights and learns a low-rank update, which reduces the number of trainable parameters by up to 10,000 times and the memory requirement by 3 times, without degrading quality or adding inference latency. We hope that LoRA will make it easier to adapt large models to many downstream tasks and to share adapted models at low cost.

papers.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
papers.short_title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
papers.abstract: Large pre-trained language models have been shown to store factual knowledge in their parameters, and achieve state-of-the-art results when fine-tuned on downstream NLP tasks. However, their ability to access and precisely manipulate knowledge is still limited, and hence on knowledge-intensive tasks their performance lags behind task-specific architectures. Additionally, providing provenance for their decisions and updating their world knowledge remain open research problems. We introduce retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), a general-purpose fine-tuning recipe that combines pre-trained parametric and non-parametric memory for language generation. We introduce RAG models where the parametric memory is a pre-trained seq2seq model and the non-parametric memory is a dense vector index of Wikipedia, accessed with a pre-trained neural retriever. We compare two formulations, one which conditions on the same retrieved passages for the whole generated sequence (RAG-Sequence) and one which can use different passages per token (RAG-Token). On three open-domain QA tasks, our models set the state of the art, outperforming parametric seq2seq models and task-specific retrieve-and-extract architectures. On Natural Questions, RAG achieves 44.5 exact match, using a DPR retriever and a FiD-style generator with the top 5 retrieved documents.

sections.title: Introduction
paragraphs: Knowledge-intensive tasks such as open-domain question answering require a model to access and reason over a large body of world knowledge. Pre-trained language models store a surprising amount of factual knowledge in their parameters, but this knowledge is difficult to update, difficult to inspect, and often imprecise. Retrieval-augmented models address these problems by combining a parametric generator with a non-parametric memory that can be searched at inference time.

We introduce RAG, a hybrid model that conditions a seq2seq generator on documents retrieved from a dense index of Wikipedia. The retriever is a dual-encoder model trained with a maximum inner product search objective, and the generator is a pre-trained encoder-decoder model. Because the index is external, the model's knowledge can be updated by replacing the index, and the retrieved documents provide provenance for the generated answer. Figure 1 shows the overall architecture.

sections.title: Methods
paragraphs: RAG uses a question encoder to embed the input and a document encoder to embed each candidate document, and it retrieves the top-k documents by inner product. The generator then conditions on the question and the retrieved documents. We consider two ways of combining the retrieved evidence, RAG-Sequence and RAG-Token, described below.

sections.title: Retrieval Model
paragraphs: The retriever is a dense dual encoder: a BERT-based question encoder maps the question to a vector, and a BERT-based document encoder maps each document to a vector in the same space. We use a pre-trained DPR retriever and keep it fixed during the first stage of training. The retrieval distribution is computed with a softmax over inner products, as in Equation (1), and the index contains 21 million Wikipedia passages.

sections.title: Generator
paragraphs: The generator is a pre-trained sequence-to-sequence model. We use a FiD generator, which encodes the question together with each retrieved document independently and then concatenates the representations before decoding. This design scales to many retrieved documents because the encoder cost grows linearly rather than quadratically in the number of passages. We use the top 5 retrieved documents in all main experiments.

sections.title: RAG-Sequence and RAG-Token
paragraphs: In RAG-Sequence the model retrieves a set of documents once and uses the same set to generate the entire output sequence. In RAG-Token the model can attend to different documents at each decoding step, which allows it to combine evidence from several passages. Both variants are trained by maximizing the marginal likelihood over the retrieved documents, as in Equation (2). RAG-Token is more expressive, while RAG-Sequence is simpler and faster at inference time.

sections.title: Experiments
paragraphs: We evaluate RAG on open-domain question answering and on abstractive question answering. The datasets are Natural Questions, TriviaQA, WebQuestions, CuratedTrec, and MSMARCO. All models use the same Wikipedia index of 21 million passages, and we report exact match for QA and ROUGE-L for generation.

sections.title: Datasets
paragraphs: Natural Questions contains questions written by real users and answers annotated in Wikipedia. TriviaQA contains trivia questions with evidence documents. WebQuestions and CuratedTrec are smaller, older benchmarks, and MSMARCO contains questions derived from search queries. For training we use the training splits of Natural Questions and TriviaQA, and we evaluate on the development and test splits of all five datasets.

sections.title: Results
paragraphs: On Natural Questions, RAG achieves 44.5 exact match, which is state of the art among models that do not use task-specific retrieval heuristics. On TriviaQA, RAG achieves 56.8 exact match, and on WebQuestions it achieves 45.2. These results outperform both parametric seq2seq models and retrieve-and-extract pipelines. Table 1 reports the exact match scores for all five datasets.

We also find that RAG generates more specific and diverse answers than a closed-book model, and that the retrieved documents provide useful provenance. In a human evaluation, annotators preferred RAG outputs over closed-book outputs for factuality and specificity. The gains are largest on questions whose answers are rare in the training data, which is consistent with the hypothesis that retrieval supplies knowledge that the parameters do not store.

sections.title: Ablations
paragraphs: We ablate the number of retrieved documents, the choice of retriever, and the training schedule. Table 2 shows that increasing the number of documents from 1 to 5 improves exact match, while further increases give diminishing returns. Freezing the retriever during the first stage and fine-tuning it later gives the best results, and training the retriever from scratch degrades performance by more than 2 points.

sections.title: Related Work
paragraphs: Retrieval-augmented models have a long history in open-domain QA. Early systems used sparse retrieval such as TF-IDF or BM25 followed by a reader, while more recent systems use dense retrievers trained end-to-end. Our work differs from these systems in that the generator is a pre-trained seq2seq model that is fine-tuned jointly with the retriever, and in that the model can generate free-form answers rather than extract spans.

Our retriever builds on DPR, which uses a BERT-based dual encoder, and our generator builds on FiD, which fuses retrieved passages in the decoder. RAG combines these ideas and shows that joint training of retrieval and generation improves both components.

sections.title: Conclusion
paragraphs: We have presented RAG, a general-purpose retrieval-augmented generation model that combines parametric and non-parametric memory. RAG achieves state-of-the-art results on open-domain QA and produces answers with provenance. We believe that retrieval-augmented models are a promising direction for knowledge-intensive NLP, and we release our code and index to support further research.

papers.title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: We explore how generating a chain of thought, a series of intermediate reasoning steps, significantly improves the ability of large language models to perform complex reasoning. In particular, we show how such reasoning abilities emerge naturally in sufficiently large language models via a simple method called chain-of-thought prompting, where a few chain of thought demonstrations are provided as exemplars in prompting. Experiments on arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning benchmarks show that chain-of-thought prompting improves performance substantially. For instance, on the GSM8K benchmark of math word problems, chain-of-thought prompting with PaLM 540B achieves 56.9 percent solve rate, compared with 17.9 percent for standard prompting. The gains are an emergent property of model scale: chain-of-thought prompting does not help small models, but it produces large gains for models with roughly 100 billion parameters or more.

sections.title: Introduction
paragraphs: Large language models have achieved impressive performance on many natural language tasks, but they still struggle with tasks that require multi-step reasoning, such as math word problems, commonsense reasoning, and symbolic manipulation. A common approach is to fine-tune the model on a large corpus of reasoning traces, but this requires substantial annotated data and does not generalize well to new tasks.

In this paper we show that a simple prompting strategy, chain-of-thought prompting, elicits reasoning in large language models without any fine-tuning. Instead of asking the model to produce only the final answer, we provide a few exemplars in which the answer is preceded by a series of intermediate reasoning steps. The model then produces a similar chain of thought for a new question. This simple change produces large gains on arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning benchmarks, and the gains grow with model scale. Figure 1 shows an example prompt and the generated chain of thought.

sections.title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting
paragraphs: Chain-of-thought prompting is a few-shot prompting method. For each task we hand-write a small number of exemplars, each consisting of a question, a chain of thought, and an answer. At inference time the exemplars are prepended to the test question, and the model generates a chain of thought followed by an answer. The model is not fine-tuned; all of its parameters remain frozen.

sections.title: Method
paragraphs: We use 8 exemplars for each task. The exemplars are written in natural language and contain the intermediate calculation or reasoning steps that lead to the answer. For arithmetic tasks the chain of thought is a sequence of equations and intermediate results; for commonsense tasks it is a short natural language explanation; for symbolic tasks it is a sequence of string manipulations. The model's output is parsed by taking the last line as the answer, and the answer is compared with the gold answer after normalization.

The key difference from standard prompting is that the exemplars include the reasoning process, not only the final answer. This gives the model a template for decomposing a problem into intermediate steps, and it makes the model's computation more transparent. The prompt is a concatenation of the exemplars and the test question, and Equation (1) shows the answer being selected by the model.

sections.title: Comparison with Standard Prompting
paragraphs: Standard prompting uses the same number of exemplars but includes only the question and the answer, without the intermediate reasoning. We compare the two methods on the same models and the same tasks. Standard prompting performs well on tasks that require a single step, but it degrades sharply as the number of reasoning steps increases. Chain-of-thought prompting, by contrast, maintains high accuracy on problems that require several steps.

sections.title: Experiments
paragraphs: We evaluate chain-of-thought prompting on three families of reasoning tasks: arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning. We use the PaLM family of models, with sizes ranging from 8 billion to 540 billion parameters, as well as GPT-3 and LaMDA. All models are evaluated in the few-shot setting without fine-tuning.

sections.title: Arithmetic Reasoning
paragraphs: The arithmetic benchmarks are GSM8K, SVAMP, ASDiv, AQuA, and MAWPS. GSM8K is the most difficult, because its problems require two to eight steps of reasoning. With PaLM 540B, chain-of-thought prompting achieves 56.9 percent solve rate on GSM8K, compared with 17.9 percent for standard prompting. On SVAMP, the same model reaches 79.0 percent with chain-of-thought prompting, compared with 57.4 percent for standard prompting.

The gains are much smaller for models with fewer than 100 billion parameters. For example, PaLM 8B improves only marginally, and GPT-3 175B improves by about 10 points. This suggests that chain-of-thought reasoning is an emergent ability of scale, rather than a generic benefit of the prompt format.

sections.title: Commonsense Reasoning
paragraphs: We evaluate on CSQA, StrategyQA, and Date Understanding. Chain-of-thought prompting improves PaLM 540B from 74.5 to 79.2 on CSQA, and from 64.6 to 72.3 on StrategyQA. The improvements are smaller than on arithmetic tasks but consistent across datasets. Many of the generated chains of thought contain plausible commonsense facts, which suggests that the model is using the reasoning trace to retrieve and combine knowledge.

sections.title: Symbolic Reasoning
paragraphs: The symbolic tasks are last-letter concatenation, coin flip, and reverse string. These tasks are synthetic and require no world knowledge, which makes them a clean test of multi-step reasoning. Chain-of-thought prompting substantially improves PaLM 540B on last-letter concatenation and coin flip, reaching 91.4 percent and 94.2 percent respectively. Standard prompting remains near chance on the same tasks, which shows that the benefit is not due to memorized answers.

sections.title: Discussion
paragraphs: Why does chain-of-thought prompting work? One explanation is that the generated intermediate steps provide additional computation, effectively allowing the model to use more layers of computation before producing an answer. Another explanation is that the intermediate steps decompose a hard problem into easier sub-problems, each of which the model can solve. Both explanations are consistent with the observation that the gains grow with model scale.

sections.title: When Does It Help?
paragraphs: Chain-of-thought prompting helps most when the task requires multi-step reasoning and the model is large enough. It does not help on tasks that require a single lookup, and it can hurt on tasks where the model already performs near ceiling. The quality of the exemplars matters: exemplars with clear and correct reasoning produce better chains than exemplars with noisy reasoning.

sections.title: Limitations
paragraphs: The generated chains of thought are not guaranteed to be faithful explanations of the model's computation. The model can produce a correct answer with an incorrect chain, and it can produce a plausible chain that leads to a wrong answer. Chain-of-thought prompting also increases inference cost, because the model generates many more tokens. Finally, the method requires hand-written exemplars, which limits its applicability to new tasks.

sections.title: Related Work
paragraphs: Few-shot prompting was popularized by GPT-3, which showed that large language models can perform many tasks from a handful of examples. Subsequent work has explored prompting strategies such as scratchpads, which also elicit intermediate computation. Our work differs in that it studies the emergence of reasoning as a function of model scale and provides a systematic evaluation across three families of reasoning tasks.

Fine-tuning on reasoning traces has also been shown to improve performance, but it requires annotated data. Chain-of-thought prompting achieves similar gains without any training, which makes it much cheaper to apply to new tasks.

sections.title: Conclusion
paragraphs: We have shown that chain-of-thought prompting, a simple few-shot prompting method, elicits multi-step reasoning in large language models. On arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning tasks, the method produces large gains for models with roughly 100 billion parameters or more. We hope that this work encourages further study of how reasoning abilities emerge with scale, and of how generated reasoning traces can be used to verify model outputs.
