papers.title: A Survey of Large Language Models: Progress, Challenges and Future Directions
papers.short_title: A Survey of Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models have become the dominant paradigm in natural language processing and are rapidly spreading to vision, speech, and scientific discovery. This survey organizes the field along four axes: architecture and pre-training, adaptation and alignment, reasoning and evaluation, and deployment. We review the progression from the Transformer to modern decoder-only models with hundreds of billions of parameters, and we trace the parallel development of vision transformers, parameter-efficient adaptation, and retrieval-augmented generation. We then discuss the open challenges of factual reliability, long-context reasoning, efficiency, safety, and evaluation, and we outline five future research directions. Our goal is to provide a coherent map of the field for researchers entering it and for practitioners choosing architectures and adaptation strategies.

sections.title: Introduction
paragraphs: Large language models have changed the practice of natural language processing. A single pre-trained model can now be adapted to translation, summarization, question answering, code generation, and dialogue with little or no task-specific training. This success has been driven by three factors: the Transformer architecture, large-scale pre-training on web-scale corpora, and scaling laws that predict performance from compute and model size.

The field has grown quickly, and the literature is now fragmented across architecture papers, adaptation methods, evaluation benchmarks, and deployment reports. This survey provides a unified view. Section 2 reviews the foundations, Section 3 compares model families, Section 4 covers adaptation, Section 5 discusses reasoning and evaluation, Section 6 surveys applications, Section 7 lists challenges, and Section 8 lays out future directions.

Our scope is deliberately broad. We include encoder-only models such as BERT, decoder-only models such as the GPT series, vision transformers, parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA, and retrieval-augmented models such as RAG. We emphasize ideas that have proven durable rather than reporting every benchmark number, and we point readers to the original papers for experimental details.

sections.title: Background and Foundations
paragraphs: The modern era of language modeling begins with the Transformer, which replaced recurrence with self-attention and made training on long sequences parallelizable. Its encoder-decoder form was quickly adapted into encoder-only and decoder-only variants, and these three families remain the basis of most models in use today.

sections.title: The Transformer Architecture
paragraphs: The Transformer stacks multi-head self-attention and position-wise feed-forward layers with residual connections and layer normalization. Its key property is that every position can attend to every other position in a constant number of operations, which removes the sequential bottleneck of recurrent networks. The original model used six encoder and six decoder layers, eight attention heads, and a hidden size of 512, and it established state of the art on WMT translation.

Two design choices proved especially influential. First, the decoder-only variant with causal masking supports efficient autoregressive generation and scales cleanly. Second, the same block can be applied to images by treating image patches as tokens, which led to the vision transformer. We return to both in Section 3.

sections.title: Pre-training Objectives
paragraphs: Encoder-only models such as BERT are trained with masked language modeling, in which a fraction of input tokens is replaced by a mask and the model predicts the original tokens. BERT also uses next-sentence prediction, and it established that bidirectional pre-training transfers well to downstream classification and span extraction. Decoder-only models instead predict the next token on a left-to-right prefix, which yields a single objective that supports both zero-shot prompting and generation.

The choice of objective shapes what the model is good at. Masked modeling produces strong representations for understanding tasks but is awkward for generation, while causal modeling produces a general-purpose generator but weaker sentence representations. Recent work attempts to combine the two, for example by using span corruption or by training with multiple objectives.

sections.title: Scaling Laws
paragraphs: Empirical scaling laws describe how loss decreases as a power law in model size, dataset size, and compute. These laws motivated the jump from hundreds of millions to hundreds of billions of parameters, including GPT-3 with 175 billion parameters and PaLM with 540 billion. They also motivate compute-optimal training, which balances parameters and tokens rather than maximizing model size alone.

Scaling laws do not by themselves explain emergent abilities, such as multi-step reasoning, that appear at particular scales. Whether emergence is a genuine discontinuity or an artifact of benchmark metrics is an open question, and it is one of the motivations for the evaluation discussion in Section 5.

A third axis is inference-time computation. Rather than increasing the number of parameters, a system can spend more compute while answering a single query by sampling several candidate chains, searching over intermediate steps, or voting across samples. Early evidence suggests that test-time compute can substitute for some of the gains normally obtained by scaling the model, particularly on reasoning tasks that reward exploration. This complicates the classical scaling-law picture, because the effective compute budget of a deployed system now includes both training and inference, and the optimal balance between the two is task dependent.

sections.title: Model Architectures
paragraphs: We group models into encoder-only, decoder-only, and vision transformer families. The grouping is useful because each family has a characteristic training objective, adaptation recipe, and set of strengths.

sections.title: Encoder-Only Models
paragraphs: BERT is the canonical encoder-only model. The base model has 12 layers, a hidden size of 768, and 12 attention heads, for 110 million parameters, while the large model has 24 layers, a hidden size of 1024, and 16 heads, for 340 million parameters. It was pre-trained on BooksCorpus and English Wikipedia with masked language modeling at a 15 percent mask rate, and it was trained on 64 TPU chips for four days.

Encoder-only models remain the best choice for tasks that require a single representation of the input, such as classification, retrieval, and span extraction. Their main limitation is that they are not directly generative, so they must be paired with a decoder or used as a component in a larger system, as in retrieval-augmented generation.

BERT is trained with two objectives: masked language modeling, which predicts randomly masked tokens from both sides of the context, and next sentence prediction, which classifies whether two segments are consecutive. Later work showed that next sentence prediction contributes little and that more data and longer training matter more than architectural changes. RoBERTa removes next sentence prediction, trains on ten times more data, and uses dynamic masking; it matches or exceeds BERT on most benchmarks with the same architecture. This line of work established a pattern that continues today: once a strong architecture exists, gains come mainly from data, scale, and training procedure.

sections.title: Decoder-Only Models
paragraphs: The GPT series established the decoder-only paradigm. GPT-1 used 117 million parameters, 12 layers, a hidden size of 768, and 12 heads, and it was pre-trained on BooksCorpus with 7000 books and then fine-tuned on downstream tasks. GPT-2 scaled to 1.5 billion parameters, 48 layers, a hidden size of 1600, 24 heads, and a context length of 1024, and it was trained on WebText, a corpus of 8 million documents totaling 40GB.

GPT-3 scaled to 175 billion parameters, 96 layers, a hidden size of 12288, 96 heads, and a context length of 2048. It was trained on 10000 NVIDIA V100 GPUs and introduced in-context few-shot learning, in which the model performs a task from examples in the prompt without any gradient updates. This shift from fine-tuning to prompting reorganized the field around a single general-purpose model.

sections.title: Vision Transformers
paragraphs: The vision transformer applies the Transformer block to images by splitting an image into 16x16 patches, embedding each patch, and treating the resulting sequence as tokens. The largest variant, ViT-H/14, has 632 million parameters and 32 Transformer layers, and it reaches 88.55 percent top-1 accuracy on ImageNet when pre-trained on JFT-300M. Training used 32 TPUv3 cores.

Vision transformers showed that the architectural advantage of attention is not specific to text. They also illustrated the importance of data scale: on small datasets, convolutional networks such as ResNet remain competitive, and the transformer advantage appears only with large-scale pre-training.

sections.title: Adaptation and Alignment
paragraphs: Pre-training is only the first stage. Adapting a model to a task, a domain, or a set of human preferences is now a research area in its own right, because full fine-tuning becomes expensive as models grow.

sections.title: Fine-Tuning and Instruction Tuning
paragraphs: Full fine-tuning updates all parameters on a task-specific dataset and remains a strong baseline. Instruction tuning instead trains on a mixture of tasks phrased as instructions, which improves zero-shot generalization to unseen instructions. Reinforcement learning from human feedback adds a reward model trained on human comparisons and is widely used to align model outputs with user preferences.

sections.title: Parameter-Efficient Adaptation
paragraphs: LoRA freezes the pre-trained weights and learns a low-rank update for each adapted matrix. On GPT-3 175B it trains only 4.7 million parameters with rank r = 8 and scaling alpha = 16, reduces GPU memory by 3 times, and adds no inference latency because the update can be merged into the weights. Adapter layers and prefix tuning are related methods that insert small trainable modules or prepend trainable vectors, but both add inference cost.

Parameter-efficient methods are now the default for adapting large models to many tasks, because they make it practical to store and serve thousands of task-specific variants from a single base model.

From a systems perspective, parameter-efficient adaptation changes the economics of serving. A single base model can remain resident in memory while many small adapters are swapped per request, which reduces the memory footprint relative to keeping one full model per task. Adapters can also be versioned and rolled back independently of the base weights, which simplifies deployment. The main open questions are how to compose several adapters without interference and whether low-rank updates remain sufficient as base models continue to grow.

sections.title: Retrieval Augmentation
paragraphs: Retrieval-augmented generation pairs a parametric generator with a non-parametric index. RAG retrieves the top 5 documents from a dense index of 21 million Wikipedia passages and conditions a FiD-style generator on them, reaching 44.5 exact match on Natural Questions with a DPR retriever. Because the knowledge lives in the index, it can be updated without retraining the model, and the retrieved passages provide provenance for the answer.

Retrieval also complements long-context models: instead of forcing the model to attend over hundreds of thousands of tokens, a retriever can select the relevant passages first. The two approaches are likely to be combined rather than to replace each other.

sections.title: Reasoning and Evaluation
paragraphs: Reasoning and evaluation are tightly coupled: as models improve on standard benchmarks, the benchmarks themselves become saturated, and new evaluations are needed to measure progress.

sections.title: Prompting and Chain-of-Thought
paragraphs: Chain-of-thought prompting asks the model to produce intermediate reasoning steps before the final answer. With PaLM 540B, it raises the GSM8K solve rate from 17.9 percent to 56.9 percent, and it produces large gains on commonsense and symbolic reasoning tasks. The gains are an emergent property of scale: they are small for models below roughly 100 billion parameters.

Chain-of-thought prompting is not a guarantee of faithful reasoning. Models can produce correct answers from incorrect chains, and they can produce plausible chains that lead to wrong answers. Verifying reasoning traces is therefore an active research problem.

Prompting has also become a design interface for applications. A fixed prompt can be evaluated and versioned like code, and small changes in wording or examples can shift accuracy by several points. This sensitivity makes prompt engineering labor intensive and motivates automatic prompt optimization, which searches over instructions and demonstrations using a validation set. Even so, prompts are brittle across model versions, so production systems usually combine prompting with retrieval and with lightweight fine-tuning of the base model.

sections.title: Benchmarks and Their Limits
paragraphs: Benchmarks such as MMLU, GSM8K, HumanEval, and HELM measure different capabilities, and no single benchmark captures general competence. Contamination between pre-training data and test sets is a persistent concern, and leaderboard overfitting can make progress look faster than it is. We recommend reporting evaluation details, including prompt format, decoding settings, and contamination checks.

sections.title: Applications
paragraphs: Large language models are now used in search, customer support, software engineering, education, and scientific research. In search and question answering, retrieval-augmented models provide answers with citations. In software engineering, models generate, explain, and test code. In science, they assist with literature review, data extraction, and hypothesis generation.

Deployment patterns differ by application. High-stakes domains such as medicine and law require human review and strong provenance, while low-stakes domains can tolerate more automation. The common requirement is evaluation: every deployment needs a task-specific test set and a monitoring plan for distribution shift.

Multimodal applications are the next frontier. Models that accept images, audio, and text are being deployed in accessibility tools, medical imaging, and robotics. These systems raise new evaluation questions, because correctness may depend on the interaction between modalities, and they require data pipelines that align modalities at scale. Early results suggest that the same transformer backbone can serve all of them, which is one reason the architecture has proved so durable.

sections.title: Challenges
paragraphs: The first challenge is factual reliability. Models can hallucinate fluent but incorrect content, and retrieval reduces but does not eliminate this problem. The second challenge is long-context reasoning: attention cost grows quadratically with sequence length, and models do not reliably use information in the middle of long contexts.

The third challenge is efficiency. Training and serving hundred-billion-parameter models require substantial compute, and parameter-efficient adaptation only partly addresses the cost. The fourth challenge is safety and governance: models can produce harmful content, leak private data, or be misused, and the norms for auditing and disclosure are still being developed.

The fifth challenge is evaluation. Static benchmarks saturate, contamination is hard to rule out, and human evaluation is expensive. Progress on all five challenges requires better measurement as much as better models.

A sixth challenge is data governance. Pre-training corpora are large, poorly documented, and often contain personal or copyrighted material, which creates legal and ethical exposure for researchers and deployers alike. Data provenance, opt-out mechanisms, and reproducible documentation of filtering decisions are therefore becoming part of model development rather than an afterthought. Addressing this challenge requires collaboration between technical teams, legal experts, and the communities whose data is used.

sections.title: Future Work
paragraphs: We identify five directions that we expect to shape the next phase of research. First, efficient long-context architectures. Attention alternatives, state-space models, and retrieval hybrids should be compared under a common protocol that measures both quality and cost at context lengths beyond one million tokens.

Second, faithful reasoning and verification. Chain-of-thought traces are useful but not guaranteed to reflect the model's computation. Future work should develop verifiers that check intermediate steps, and should study when generated explanations can be trusted.

Third, retrieval and tool use. Retrieval-augmented generation has shown that external memory improves factuality, but current systems retrieve once and generate once. Future systems should interleave retrieval, tool calls, and generation, and should learn when to retrieve and when to rely on parameters.

Fourth, multimodal grounding. Vision transformers and multimodal models have made rapid progress, but grounding language in perception, action, and structured data remains difficult. Benchmarks that require spatial, temporal, and causal reasoning across modalities are needed.

Fifth, safety, evaluation, and governance. As models are deployed in high-stakes settings, we need auditable evaluations, provenance for generated content, and mechanisms for redressing harm. Technical work on watermarking, uncertainty estimation, and interpretability should be paired with policy work on disclosure and accountability.

sections.title: Conclusion
paragraphs: Large language models have advanced rapidly because architecture, data, and scale improved together. The Transformer provided a scalable block, pre-training provided a general objective, and scaling provided predictable gains. Adaptation methods, retrieval, and prompting then turned a single pre-trained model into a platform for many tasks.

The remaining challenges are substantial. Factual reliability, long-context reasoning, efficiency, safety, and evaluation all require sustained work. We hope that this survey provides a useful map of the field and a clear statement of the open problems that matter most.

appendix.title: Appendix: Method Notes
paragraphs: This appendix records how papers were selected and how numbers were checked. We searched for architecture, adaptation, reasoning, and evaluation papers published between 2012 and 2024, and we retained papers that introduced a widely used method or that reported a result cited by later work. We gave priority to papers with public code and to papers whose results have been reproduced.

All parameter counts and benchmark numbers in the survey are taken from the original papers and are reported for the largest variant unless stated otherwise. Where a paper reports multiple settings, we use the setting that the authors describe as their main result. We did not re-run any experiments, so the numbers should be read as reported values rather than as independent replications.

The five future directions in Section 8 were chosen by clustering the limitations discussed in the papers we reviewed. They are not intended to be exhaustive. We expect the relative importance of the directions to change as models, benchmarks, and deployment practices evolve.

appendix.title: Appendix: Glossary
paragraphs: Fine-tuning: updating all model parameters on a task-specific dataset. Instruction tuning: fine-tuning on a mixture of tasks phrased as instructions. Parameter-efficient adaptation: adapting a model while training only a small number of additional parameters. Retrieval augmentation: conditioning generation on documents retrieved from an external index. Chain-of-thought prompting: few-shot prompting in which exemplars include intermediate reasoning steps.

papers.title: Understanding Deep Learning: Chapter 1 - Introduction
papers.abstract: This chapter introduces deep learning as the study of models with many layers of computation that are learned from data. It defines the supervised learning problem, explains why depth is useful, and reviews the historical developments that made deep networks practical. The chapter closes with an overview of the book and guidance on how to read it. No prior background in machine learning is assumed beyond basic linear algebra, calculus, and probability.

sections.title: Introduction
paragraphs: Deep learning is a subfield of machine learning that studies models composed of many layers of simple computations. Each layer transforms its input into a representation that is more useful for the task at hand, and the parameters of all layers are learned jointly from data. The word deep refers to the number of layers, not to any claim about the depth of understanding achieved by the model.

This book is about how such models work. It explains the building blocks, the training algorithms, and the design choices that determine whether a network learns well or fails. The emphasis is on ideas that generalize across applications, not on the details of any particular benchmark. Figure 1 shows the place of deep learning within artificial intelligence and machine learning.

A reader who finishes the book should be able to implement a small deep network from scratch, understand why it trains or does not train, and read the research literature with confidence. The book assumes familiarity with vectors, matrices, derivatives, and basic probability, but it does not assume prior exposure to neural networks.

sections.title: What is Deep Learning?
paragraphs: In supervised learning we are given a training set of input-output pairs (x_i, y_i), and we want to find a function f that maps inputs to outputs and generalizes to new inputs. A deep network represents f as a composition of layers, f(x) = f_L(f_(L-1)(...f_1(x)...)), where each layer has its own parameters. The composition is what gives the model its expressive power: a deep network can represent functions that would require an exponentially large shallow network to approximate.

The parameters are chosen by minimizing a loss function that measures the mismatch between predictions and targets, as in Equation (1). For regression the loss is usually squared error; for classification it is usually cross-entropy. The optimizer adjusts the parameters by gradient descent, and the gradients are computed efficiently by backpropagation.

Deep learning differs from classical machine learning in that the representation itself is learned. In a classical pipeline, a human engineer designs features and the model learns a simple mapping from features to outputs. In a deep network, the features are learned by the earlier layers and the final layer learns the mapping. This end-to-end approach is the main reason deep networks outperform classical pipelines when data is plentiful.

A useful way to think about a deep network is as a stack of representation learners. Each layer maps its input into a new coordinate system in which the prediction task is simpler. The lower layers are shared across tasks, while the upper layers specialize. This division of labor is why a network trained on one task can often be fine-tuned on another with few labeled examples, and it is the idea behind the transfer learning methods discussed in later chapters.

Deep learning is not limited to supervised learning. Unsupervised methods learn structure from unlabeled data, and reinforcement learning learns from rewards. The supervised setting is emphasized here because it is the cleanest way to introduce the mechanics of layers, losses, and gradients, and because most of the techniques carry over to the other settings. Figure 3 shows the computation performed by a single neuron.

sections.title: A Brief History
paragraphs: The idea of learning from data with layered models is old. The perceptron, introduced in the late 1950s, was a single-layer linear classifier, and its limitations were famously analyzed in the 1960s. Multilayer networks and backpropagation became popular in the 1980s, but they were difficult to train at scale and fell out of favor in the 1990s.

Three developments revived the field. First, large labeled datasets such as ImageNet made it possible to train models with millions of parameters. Second, graphics processing units made the arithmetic fast enough to train such models in reasonable time. Third, improved activation functions, initialization schemes, and regularization methods made deep networks trainable.

The turning point was the AlexNet result on ImageNet in 2012, which reduced the top-5 error rate to 15.3 percent and beat the previous best by a large margin. The network had 60 million parameters and eight layers, and it was trained on two GTX 580 GPUs for five to six days. Subsequent work introduced residual connections, which made it possible to train networks with more than one hundred layers, and attention-based architectures, which now dominate language modeling.

The years after 2012 brought a steady sequence of architectural innovations. Batch normalization made deeper convolutional networks easier to optimize, residual connections removed the degradation problem, and generative adversarial networks introduced a new training paradigm. Recurrent networks with attention dominated sequence modeling until 2017, when the Transformer replaced recurrence with self-attention. Transformer-based models then scaled from millions to hundreds of billions of parameters, and the same recipe was adapted to images, audio, and multimodal data. This history matters because many current design choices are responses to practical failures of earlier architectures rather than purely theoretical advances.

sections.title: Why Depth Matters
paragraphs: Depth is useful because many functions of interest have a compositional structure. A face is composed of eyes, a nose, and a mouth; a sentence is composed of words, phrases, and clauses. A deep network can reuse intermediate representations across tasks, so the number of parameters needed to represent a compositional function grows more slowly with depth than with width.

Depth also enables abstraction. Earlier layers learn low-level features such as edges and textures, middle layers learn parts and motifs, and later layers learn objects and concepts. This hierarchy is not imposed by hand; it emerges from training on data. Visualization studies of convolutional networks provided some of the earliest evidence for this behavior.

Depth is not free. Deeper networks are harder to optimize, more expensive to train, and more prone to overfitting when data is limited. The rest of the book is largely about the techniques that make deep networks trainable: careful initialization, normalization, residual connections, and regularization.

A second reason depth helps is parameter efficiency. A deep network can represent a function as a composition of simpler functions, and for many structured functions the number of parameters needed grows linearly with depth, whereas a shallow network may need exponentially many units in its width. This argument is informal, but it matches practice: deep convolutional networks outperform shallow ones with comparable parameter counts on image recognition, and deep transformers outperform shallow ones on language tasks at fixed parameter budgets. Depth is therefore not merely a way to add capacity; it changes how capacity is organized.

sections.title: Overview of the Book
paragraphs: The book is organized into four parts. Part I introduces the supervised learning problem and the basic building blocks of neural networks. Part II covers training: loss functions, gradients, backpropagation, and optimization. Part III covers architectures for images, sequences, and sets, including convolutional networks, recurrent networks, and transformers. Part IV covers advanced topics such as generative models, reinforcement learning, and ethics.

Each chapter includes worked examples, exercises, and pointers to the literature. The exercises are graded from conceptual questions to implementation tasks, and solutions are available to instructors. The book's website hosts code notebooks that reproduce the figures.

The chapters are designed to be read in order, but they are also modular. A reader interested in training can start with Part II and return to Part I for notation; a reader interested in applications can read Part III after Chapter 2. Each part ends with a short summary and a set of exercises that connect the ideas to practice. Supplementary material on the website includes datasets, code, and a glossary.

sections.title: The Supervised Learning Problem
paragraphs: This section formalizes the supervised learning problem and introduces the notation used throughout the book. We distinguish between the training loss, which is minimized on the training set, and the test loss, which measures generalization to unseen data.

The central challenge is that minimizing training loss does not guarantee low test loss. A model with enough parameters can memorize the training set, achieving zero training loss while generalizing poorly. Regularization, data augmentation, and early stopping are all ways to control this trade-off.

sections.title: Loss Functions
paragraphs: A loss function assigns a scalar cost to a prediction. For regression, the squared error loss is differentiable and easy to optimize, but it is sensitive to outliers. For classification, the cross-entropy loss is the standard choice because it is the negative log-likelihood of the correct class under a softmax model.

The choice of loss should reflect the cost of errors in the application. In medical diagnosis, a false negative may be much worse than a false positive, and the loss should encode that asymmetry. In many cases the right loss is not the one that is easiest to optimize.

Loss functions also determine the scale of the gradients. Squared error produces gradients proportional to the prediction error, so learning slows as the error shrinks; cross-entropy produces gradients proportional to the difference between the predicted probability and the target, which stays informative even when the model is confident and wrong. This difference is one reason cross-entropy is preferred for classification, and it illustrates a general principle: the loss should be chosen together with the output activation, not independently. Table 2 lists the notation used throughout the book. The parameters themselves are updated by gradient descent, as in Equation (2).

A loss function is usually averaged over the training set, so its scale depends on the number of examples. When comparing losses across datasets, it is therefore better to report per-example averages than sums. The same care applies to reported accuracies: a number without its dataset, split, and evaluation protocol is difficult to interpret.

sections.title: Training and Testing
paragraphs: We split the available data into a training set, a validation set, and a test set. The training set is used to fit the parameters, the validation set is used to choose hyperparameters, and the test set is used only once to estimate generalization. Using the test set for model selection is a common mistake that leads to optimistic estimates.

When data is scarce, cross-validation provides a more efficient use of the available examples. The training data is divided into folds, and each fold is held out in turn while the model is trained on the remaining folds. The average validation loss across folds is then used for model selection.

Choosing the split between training, validation, and test data is itself a modeling decision. If the same distribution is used for all three, performance estimates can be optimistic, because subtle leakage through preprocessing or duplicate examples inflates test accuracy. A clean protocol fixes the split before any model is trained, tunes hyperparameters only on the validation set, and reports the test set once. When data is scarce, cross-validation reuses examples across folds at the cost of additional computation.

A final practical issue is distribution shift. A model trained on one population may encounter a different population after deployment, and accuracy can degrade sharply even when the new data looks similar to a human. Monitoring input statistics and re-evaluating on recent data are therefore part of the lifecycle of a deployed model, not a one-time check performed before release.

sections.title: Summary
paragraphs: Deep learning studies models with many layers of learned representation. Depth provides compositionality and abstraction, but it also makes optimization harder. The field's recent success depends on large datasets, fast hardware, and training techniques that keep deep networks stable.

The next chapter introduces the simplest deep network, the fully connected network, and shows how to train it on a small classification problem. Later chapters build on this foundation to cover convolutional networks, sequence models, and transformers.

The chapter has introduced the vocabulary and the questions that the rest of the book answers. The key idea is that depth turns a hard function into a composition of easier functions, and that learning succeeds when data, optimization, and regularization are balanced. The remaining chapters make each of these ingredients precise.
